sections.h2: Where is Montgomery County and what does its housing market look like?
sections.html:
Hillsboro is the seat of Montgomery County, which lies in south-central Illinois, and Litchfield is its biggest city. It was formed in 1821 from parts of Bond and Madison counties and named for Richard Montgomery, a Revolutionary War general. Seven counties touch its edges: Sangamon, Christian, Shelby, Fayette, Bond, Madison and Macoupin, and roughly 704 square miles of it is land.

Headcount slid from 30,104 in 2010 to 28,288 in 2020, with a July 2025 estimate of 28,076. Values are modest, yet a seller still has to clear every open tax installment before closing.

Around Hillsboro, January lows average near 21 degrees and July highs near 91, so roofs and foundations take cycles of freezing and baking. Buyers' inspectors tend to look hard at both.

sections.h2: Who do you call in Montgomery County about a tax question?
sections.html:
Four desks split the work, and each answers a different question:

  • Treasurer and ex-officio collector: mails and collects real estate, drainage and mobile home tax, and runs the yearly sale. Find it at Room 101, 1 Courthouse Square, Hillsboro, phone (217) 532-9521.
  • County Clerk and Recorder: works out each parcel's rate, handles redemption of sold taxes and records deeds. Rate and redemption calls go to (217) 532-9530, recording to (217) 532-9535.
  • Supervisor of Assessments: runs the assessment cycle, processes exemptions and looks up parcel numbers. It is in Room 201 at (217) 532-9595.
  • Board of Review: hears complaints about value, in the Supervisor's suite.

Valuation questions start with the township assessor, and bills with the Treasurer. Calling the right desk first saves a transfer.

sections.h2: How do you pay a Montgomery County tax bill?
sections.html:
The Treasurer accepts five routes, all listed on the office page:

  • Mail, addressed to the Treasurer at 1 Courthouse Square, Room 101, Hillsboro, IL 62049.
  • Walk in at Room 101 of the Historic Courthouse.
  • A gray metal drop box by the fire escape, north face of the courthouse.
  • The automated line, (217) 627-6183.
  • The online link posted on the Treasurer's page.

Under Public Act 104-0553 the county now buys its own delinquent real estate taxes as trustee for the districts, beginning with the sale for tax year 2025. Delinquent mobile home taxes still go to private bidders. Owners who like to pay early can ask about the prepayment contract. The deposit sits in trust against the coming bill, a shortfall is due by the second due date, extra money is refunded, and the interest stays with the county.

sections.h2: What deadlines apply to a Montgomery County bill?
sections.html:
Each year's bill prints its own dates, so read the stubs. Under state law the first installment turns delinquent after the later of June 1 and the day following its printed date, and the second after the later of September 1 and the day following its printed date (35 ILCS 200/21-15). Interest runs at 1 1/2% for each month or fraction.

Mail with a postmark by the deadline counts as timely. The county's FAQ adds that tax is owed even if no bill shows up, so a new owner who never got one should phone the Treasurer for the figure and ask who is listed as taxpayer of record.

One more point from the Supervisor's page: the name printed on a bill is there for mailing. Ownership is shown by the last deed on file with the Recorder.

sections.h2: How does Montgomery County turn a home's value into a tax figure?
sections.html:
Township assessors set values, and equalization factors from the Supervisor's office pull the level to 33 1/3 percent of market. Subtract exemptions and you have the base the levies hit. Every district certifies what it needs, the Clerk converts that into a rate, and rate times equalized value is the tax.

A district may lift its levy up to 5 percent over what it collected the prior year; more than that forces a Truth-in-Taxation hearing, which is informational and needs no vote. When a bill climbs, the Clerk's page names three suspects: a higher rate, a higher assessment, or an exemption you are missing.

Special areas add wrinkles. A parcel inside a TIF district owes the same total, but part flows to the TIF fund. Drainage charges are set by the district with court approval, and an annexed parcel takes on the new district's rate.

sections.h2: How can an owner contest a value in Montgomery County?
sections.html:
Talk to the township assessor, then the Supervisor at (217) 532-9595, and go formal only if the answers do not satisfy you. The Board sits starting the first Monday of June, with extra meetings as the workload requires. Statute sets a 30 calendar day window after the assessment list is published (35 ILCS 200/16-55).

The Clerk's page names a second route for the current year's tax: an objection lodged with the Circuit Clerk, (217) 532-9546. Protests aimed at future years go to the Board through the Supervisor. The paths differ, so ask which one fits before paying any fee.

Either way, the dispute concerns value rather than the dollar tax. The Supervisor also invites neighbors to report a property that looks under-assessed, since errors in either direction shift the rate for everyone.

sections.h2: What follows an unpaid Montgomery County bill?
sections.html:
Whatever stays unpaid goes to the Treasurer's annual sale. Afterward the owner can still redeem for two to three years, depending on property type, though interest and fees make it costlier.

  • The Clerk issues an Estimate of Redemption; check that it names the right parcel.
  • Pay in cash, certified funds or a money order to the Montgomery County Clerk. No payment plans exist.
  • Miss the next year's second installment and the buyer may purchase that year too, at 12%.
  • Tax deed process costs are added to the redemption figure.

After a sale the Clerk's office mails a notice called a Take Notice, and the delinquent list runs in local papers beforehand. Keep a copy of every check or receipt, which the county calls the best defense if a payment is not credited.

sections.h2: Which exemptions help a Montgomery County homeowner?
sections.html:
The general homestead exemption covers an owner's principal residence, capped at a $6,000 cut in equalized value for counties of this kind (35 ILCS 200/15-175). The Supervisor's office also helps applicants complete the Senior Homestead Exemption and the Senior Citizens Assessment Freeze forms.

The freeze form is refiled annually, since household income shifts when someone moves in or out. Ask the Supervisor's office which forms you need after a move.

sections.h2: What should a Montgomery County seller line up before closing?
sections.html:
Gather the parcel number, request current and prior bills from the Treasurer, and ask the Clerk if any year was sold. The title company prorates the current year, and the settlement statement shows what is paid or owed.

The deed must also pass the Recorder's checklist: street address and parcel number beside the legal description, a notarized Plat Act Affidavit, and a "future taxes to" name and address. Margins are specific, with a two inch gap on page one's upper right and one inch on later pages. The description printed on a tax bill is not a full legal description and will be refused.

A free Property Fraud Alert sign-up from the Recorder notifies you by email or phone whenever a document is recorded under your name, a sensible safeguard around a sale.

faqs.q: Who answers Treasurer questions in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: The Treasurer's office, at (217) 532-9521 in Room 101 of the Historic Courthouse, also supplies copies of current or past bills. Card and phone payments run through (217) 627-6183.

faqs.q: Is there a payment plan to redeem sold Montgomery County taxes?
faqs.a: No. The County Clerk accepts only cash, certified funds or a money order and offers no installments on redemption. Request an Estimate of Redemption at (217) 532-9530 before sending money.

faqs.q: Who calculates the rate on my bill?
faqs.a: The County Clerk does. Each taxing body certifies a levy, the Clerk's staff divides it by the valuation within statutory limits, and the Treasurer prints and mails the result.

faqs.q: Is the name on my bill proof of ownership?
faqs.a: No. The Supervisor of Assessments says the bill's name and address serve mailing only, and the last recorded deed identifies the owner.

faqs.q: Where does an assessment complaint go?
faqs.a: It goes to the Board of Review through the Supervisor of Assessments, (217) 532-9595, within 30 calendar days of the list's publication.
